title: Present in every land
hook: the Jaap salutes the One who dwells in every country and every garb

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhai, without fear, and your line, fearless like him. Today, Jaap looks out across the whole map.

Open a map of gurdwaras on your phone and zoom out. Southall, in west London. Surrey, near Vancouver. Yuba City in California. Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur, Melbourne, Singapore, a small town in northern Italy. Behind each little marker, someone who left Punjab, carried the Guru's words in a suitcase, and found that the morning prayers still worked in a new time zone. Long before any of that, the Tenth Guru wrote praise that fits every one of those places.
screen: `A MAP OF GURDWARAS, ZOOMED OUT.` → `MARKERS SCATTERED ACROSS THE MAP.` → `THE PRAYERS WORK IN A NEW TIME ZONE.`

segments.voice: Throughout Jaap, the One is saluted as dwelling everywhere: in every country, in every kind of dress, in water and on land. One short chachari line says it in four words: jale hain, thale hain. You are in the water. You are on the land. And near its very end, Jaap calls the One chatar chakkar vartee, present in all four directions, every point of the compass. Think about what every garb meant in the Guru's world. Clothing told everyone who you were: a Hindu holy man's saffron, a Muslim scholar's robe, a soldier's armor, a farmer's rough cotton, a queen's silk. Jaap salutes the One in all of them, and Sikhs read it plainly: no land is holier by birth, and no costume is closer to the Divine. Sikhs have long lived that line. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak walking for years, east toward Assam, south toward Sri Lanka, north into the mountains, west as far as Mecca and Baghdad, sitting with people of every faith he met. And today Sikhs pray the Ardas in Toronto and Birmingham and Bangkok with the same closing words you met at the end of year one: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of Punjab. The good of all. In that reading, every land is somewhere to pray, and every stranger in every garb is someone the One is already with.
screen: `EVERY COUNTRY, EVERY GARB.` · `JALE HAIN, THALE HAIN: WATER AND LAND.` · `CHATAR CHAKKAR VARTEE: ALL DIRECTIONS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `IN EVERY LAND.`

segments.voice: Choose a faraway place, somewhere you've never been, somewhere in the news, or the place your family came from, and picture the people there waking up or going to sleep right now. Breathe in and picture them; breathe out and wish them well, plainly: may they be safe, may they be fed. If you pray, you can hold them in the words sarbat da bhala.
Des. A country or land — Jaap salutes the One in every des and every garb, in water and on land, in all four directions.
Your line: in every land. No place is too far for the good of all. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 353 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BEYOND THE FEAR OF DEATH.`

howItsDone: Sikhs around the world recite Jaap Sahib in the same words every morning, and gurdwaras far from Punjab close their gatherings with the Ardas's prayer for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

original.note: Gurmukhi: des, a country or land; Jaap salutes the One in every des and every bhes, garb.

trapdoor: what you thought: present in every land means God is everywhere, vaguely.
what it means: no land or costume is closer to the One; every place is somewhere to pray, every stranger someone the One is with.
what a scholar hears: Jaap's des/bhes pairing and jale hain, thale hain express sarab viapak (all-pervading); chatar chakkar vartee recurs in the final stanza.

chat.says: Are Sikh prayers mainly for Punjab, or do they fit anywhere in the world?
options: Anywhere: Jaap salutes the One in every land and garb, in water and on land.
Mainly Punjab; the prayers work best in the Guru's own land and language.
Anywhere, but only inside a gurdwara built just like the ones in Punjab.
chat.meaning: Jaap salutes the One in every country and every garb, jale hain, thale hain, and the Ardas asks sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

jale.meaning: in the water; jale hain, You are in the water

thale.meaning: on the land; thale hain, You are on the land

Ardas.meaning: the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings

sarbat da bhala.meaning: the good of all, the Ardas's closing words
